name: Solar Power

claims.claim_text: Making the crystalline silicon for solar cells is an energy-intensive multi-stage chemical process: sand is reduced with coal into a slag, dissolved in acid, reacted to produce silane gas, deposited as pure silicon onto rods in reactors, then remelted and drawn into a boule.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then this acid, you do a reaction with it that produces silane gas. And then you run it into these reactors that deposit out pure silicon on these long rods. And then you take that and you remelt it again.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Stacked incentives can dominate residential solar economics: an Oregon Energy Trust incentive covered about a third of one system's cost, state and federal credits covered slightly more than another third, leaving $4,300 out of pocket.
claims.quote_verbatim: we were able to get officially this system incentive from the Oregon Energy Trust that paid about a third of the cost. And then the state and federal paid another about a little over that third. And what was left was $4,300 out-of-pocket expenses.
claims.speaker: Bob Simpson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Simpson - Ardent Automotive Artisan

claims.claim_text: Installed residential arrays can beat their contractual production guarantee: one Portland system guaranteed 4.8 MWh per year and actually delivered 5.26 MWh in its first full year.
claims.quote_verbatim: And they guaranteed 4.8 megawatt hours of energy off of this panel. And it turns out I got 5.26 megawatt hours off of it.
claims.speaker: Bob Simpson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Simpson - Ardent Automotive Artisan

claims.claim_text: A well-to-wheels spreadsheet study covering coal mining, diesel hauling, plant conversion, 7.5 percent delivery loss into the garage and charger losses found an EV charged entirely from coal-fired grid power produced about 27 percent less CO2 than burning the equivalent gasoline, benchmarked at 19.2 pounds of CO2 per gallon.
claims.quote_verbatim: the number turned out to be 27% less CO2 produced if 100% of the energy that I drive with came from coal put onto the power grid
claims.speaker: Bob Simpson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Simpson - Ardent Automotive Artisan

claims.claim_text: An Australian 1.5 kW residential system cost about four thousand dollars once the large early government subsidy had been wound back.
claims.quote_verbatim: It cost us about four grand, I think, for a one and a half kilowatt system. I mean, we should have got it when the government subsidy was massive and you practically got the thing for free.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: Australian feed-in tariffs inverted from paying about three times the retail rate to paying about one quarter of it, which flips the economics from exporting to self-consuming daytime generation.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because the feed-in tariff is like one quarter of what you actually pay. Right. Whereas it used to be three times.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: Feed-in tariffs come in net and gross variants: net pays only for the surplus exported after the house consumes what it needs, while gross pays for all generation regardless of on-site use.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's two systems, net and gross. I'm on net. Yeah. What that means is that I only get paid for the excess energy I put back.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar, FPGAs and Maxim Integrated - Solar Shopper Sickness

claims.claim_text: Conventional generators earn disproportionately at peak, when extra turbines are brought online on hot days, so distributed solar that shaves those peaks undermines the revenue model the grid is financed on.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of their money is made actually at peak times. So, like, when a hot summer day, they flip a switch, they turn on an extra turbine, and that's actually when they start cranking out all the money
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Solar, FPGAs and Maxim Integrated - Solar Shopper Sickness

claims.claim_text: Battery-plus-solar sensors embedded in roadway concrete avoid cutting the asphalt for wiring and can run five years before needing maintenance, which is what makes fire-and-forget deployment practical.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's all battery and solar power. You fire and forget. You deploy and it goes for five years before it needs any maintenance.
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: Greg Charvat Returns With A Book! - Laboratory Literature Laureate

claims.claim_text: Germany became the first country to briefly supply half its electricity from solar, a milestone reached despite unremarkable solar irradiation.
claims.quote_verbatim: Germany first country to hit 50% of their energy comes from solar.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar Factories and HVDC Lines - Pollent Power Pushing

claims.claim_text: Tree shading has historically been the blocking constraint for residential installs in wooded neighborhoods, but newer panel-level electronics make shaded roofs workable.
claims.quote_verbatim: There are trees all around the place and that up until now has been a challenge. But the technologies which are being released right now allow you to get around that.
claims.speaker: Martin Lorton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Martin Lorton - Variegated Video Vagility

claims.claim_text: Where the local utility will not buy exported energy and the interconnection paperwork is heavy, the rational design choice is a system that never feeds the grid at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm setting my system up not to feed into the grid because at the moment, as far as I can tell, the electric company here isn't going to buy it back.
claims.speaker: Martin Lorton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Martin Lorton - Variegated Video Vagility

claims.claim_text: A solar-powered factory that must run continuously forces its owner into grid-scale storage, since production and 24/7 demand do not coincide.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're going to power the factory by a solar and they're going to have to run their factory 24-7. So no wonder they're getting into grid storage.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Risky Components and Hardware Innovation - Slipshod Shack Shutdown

claims.claim_text: Among ambient energy sources, a few square inches of solar cell with battery backup is the most successful harvesting approach, with thermoelectric generation second and mechanical harvesting rarely working out; the right choice is highly application specific, so a hot pole-mounted transformer argues for thermoelectrics.
claims.quote_verbatim: the number one energy scavenging thing has been solar with some battery backup. And then after that, it would be probably thermoelectric generation.
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Wearable-sized solar cells cannot collect enough energy to meaningfully recharge a phone battery, which makes solar-powered wristband power banks an energy-budget impossibility rather than an engineering challenge.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't get enough solar power in there to, you know, charge a, charge a piece of wet string
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Glass and Gongkai GSM - Unzymotic Ursidae Upbuilding

claims.claim_text: Where grid electricity costs only eight or nine cents per kilowatt-hour, rooftop solar has no economic driver; high retail power prices are what pushed Australian rooftop penetration past 13 percent of homes.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's what drives it here in Australia. That's why like greater than 13% of homes in Australia have solar, solar roof tops.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Wearables Might Have Limited Fashion Options - Lachrymogenic Lane Language

claims.claim_text: Home servers and other deferrable loads can be gated to run only on surplus generation, either on a simple daytime timer or on an insolation threshold that switches the load in once output passes a set level.
claims.quote_verbatim: But maybe I could have like a solar insulation thing that, you know, it only switches on when it reaches a certain power output
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Gotta Update My Dog

claims.claim_text: Once solar falls below a threshold cost per watt, its deployment stops depending on policy and becomes a pure market outcome that no political decision can reverse.
claims.quote_verbatim: once solar reaches a certain power point, a certain cost per watt, it really doesn't matter what anybody does. Right. That's, that's what the market's going to do.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Work on it for 10 years...

claims.claim_text: Falling headline solar spending worldwide can mask growing deployment, because the cost per watt installed dropped; the per-watt installation figure is the number to track rather than total dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: the solar spending is down, like overall throughout the world, but that is almost exclusively because the, the, the cost of solar has dropped
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Road trip to the deep space network

claims.claim_text: A solar-powered sensor sealed inside a septic tank runs its panel on a cable out to the exterior and buffers into a lithium-ion cell; at hourly 3G uploads the reserve carries roughly two to three weeks with no sun.
claims.quote_verbatim: with the 3G kind of uploading, like maybe once per hour, then it should have a, uh, a lifetime of maybe two to three weeks of no sun
claims.speaker: Akiba
claims.episode_title: The Internet of Septage (with Akiba)

claims.claim_text: When the export tariff is negligible, appliances with timers should be scheduled into daylight hours so the generation is self-consumed rather than exported; unused daytime output is effectively wasted.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's during the day when we're pissing away the solar. If we don't use it, we lose it almost.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The EEVblog Sparkgap Generator

claims.claim_text: The 1970s push for solar failed principally on cost, and the durable argument for solar is the economic one: the system earns its cost back and then supplies power for free.
claims.quote_verbatim: speaking of Jimmy Carter and obviously the failure of the 70s to bring on the solar aside from the cost of it, whatever, is that the economic argument is the best argument there is
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Ergs Per Second

claims.claim_text: Even with costs dropping fast, solar was still under five percent of world energy supply as of the mid-2010s, which is the scale check to apply against enthusiastic growth figures.
claims.quote_verbatim: like solar is still like less than five percent you know it's growing for sure and the costs are dropping like crazy
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Grow A Superbrain

claims.claim_text: On a small satellite the available solar area is the hard outer bound on the power budget, so the design method is to drive every subsystem as low-power as possible and then trade away duty cycle, for instance by not sampling over certain regions.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's basically, we have this much energy available. We try to make everything as low power as possible. And then that's kind of what it is.
claims.speaker: Joris Aerts
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: Australia reached roughly 40 percent of houses carrying rooftop solar, the highest uptake in the world, driven by subsidies, while electric vehicles remained about 0.1 percent of car sales there.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have practically the world's largest solar uptake here because of the subsidies. We, everyone, like 40% of houses here in Australia have solar on them.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Payback period scales with equipment tier: a low-cost residential system pays back very quickly while a top-quality system takes longer, though still on the order of five years, after which the energy is effectively free.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you install like a lower cost system, your payback period's incredibly low. But if you buy like all the top quality stuff, your payback period's longer, but still it's like five years tops
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Space Time Continuum with Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: Before quoting a residential install, use a roof-modelling tool that maps usable area, energy per square area and tree shading from a 3D model; complex multi-facet roofs can be ruled out on geometry alone because panels are rectangular.
claims.quote_verbatim: it'll map how much energy square area your roof is and tell you how much your solar energy and it'll show shading for trees
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Timing is Everything

claims.claim_text: For cold-weather solar deployments, a six-volt gel cell trickle-charged from the panel is a more robust storage choice than lithium-ion, with an off-the-shelf buck converter handling the panel's higher open-circuit voltage.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I think it was like a six volt cell. Which actually goes up to like. Eight nine volts. And then you trickle charge. On a six volt gel cell.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Assembly Chat

claims.claim_text: Characterizing a solar cell properly means loading it and sweeping the curve to find its peak power point rather than taking an open-circuit voltage reading.
claims.quote_verbatim: when they're usually measuring solar cells, aren't they usually doing it by, like, loading them, like, trying to get, find the peak point and, like, actually loading them through the curve?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Here for a reason

claims.claim_text: Very high rooftop penetration creates a real operational problem: midday export pushes distribution voltages toward or past the compliant limit, which is why utilities want the ability to curtail residential systems.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's pumping too much power into the grid at certain times of the day. And, and the voltages go way above, you know, it risks the voltages going above the compliant level
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Electrical Archeology

claims.claim_text: A home battery only pays without solar if the meter supports time-of-day tariffs; on a flat-rate dumb meter, day and night power cost the same and there is no arbitrage to capture.
claims.quote_verbatim: Here, here in Australia, you've got to have a smart meter to make that viable. Right. So I, I, I don't have a smart meter. I've got a dumb meter.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Electrical Archeology

claims.claim_text: Large wind turbines do not spin synchronously with the grid, so they generate into DC and feed the grid through an inverter, unlike conventional synchronous machines.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of those wind turbines actually generate into DC, into an inverter system
claims.speaker: Paul Zawada
claims.episode_title: The Smart Grid with Paul Zawada

claims.claim_text: A 60 cent per kilowatt-hour feed-in tariff plus government subsidies drove Australian rooftop solar to about 35 percent of homes, showing how directly tariff design steers demand.
claims.quote_verbatim: they actually gave us 50 cents or it's no 60 cents per kilowatt hour feeding tariff and all these government subsidies. And so every, so now 35% of homes in this country have solar on them.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Professional Scooter Charger

claims.claim_text: In a US state with few incentives, quoted residential solar came back with an eighteen-year payback, which is the practical reason such installs get abandoned.
claims.quote_verbatim: I looked at solar and I had some people give me quotes and stuff like that. It was like 18 years. It was like really long time because of, because there's not many incentives in my state.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Professional Scooter Charger

claims.claim_text: A top-of-the-line three kilowatt Australian system bought around 2015 cost $5,000 after state and federal rebates and paid for itself in about five years.
claims.quote_verbatim: for my original three kilowatt solar power system, I, I, I paid $5,000 and that included, that was nine, eight, nine years ago now, and that included the, uh, government rebates
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Professional Scooter Charger

claims.claim_text: When a system already generates large daytime surplus, doubling the energy a daytime appliance consumes barely moves the payback period, because the extra consumption only displaces export sold at a very low rate.
claims.quote_verbatim: the payback period is basically the same because we've got so much excess solar energy that it doesn't really matter
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Picking a Pick and Place Pickiness

claims.claim_text: Aggregate household demand is highly predictable, so high solar penetration forces utilities to fold unreliable weather forecasts into generation planning, adding a new source of error that did not exist before.
claims.quote_verbatim: And now they have to tie bloody, you know, forecasts of weather into, you know, weather is not that predictable.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Picking a Pick and Place Pickiness

claims.claim_text: Having previously worked through reports concluding a fully renewable Australian grid was achievable, one long-time renewables advocate reversed position and now regards nuclear as necessary for baseload, while noting a ten-year ramp and no domestic expertise.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've gone into the numbers. I've read reports and everything that, yeah, we can do this. We can go like a hundred percent renewable energy. And now I'm thinking, nah, I think nuclear is our only way forward.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Picking a Pick and Place Pickiness

claims.claim_text: A solar-diverting EV charger regulates the car's draw by varying the pilot PWM duty cycle, and the resulting control loop has a delay of a few seconds before the vehicle compensates.
claims.quote_verbatim: So the car adjusts its charging level based on the PWM output of the thing.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Slapping Industries

claims.claim_text: Aptera's bankruptcy illustrates the economics of solar-on-vehicle: an otherwise ordinary EV with roof panels priced around a quarter of a million dollars had no viable market.
claims.quote_verbatim: Who would have thought that a very ordinary EV with solar panels strapped on the roof that cost a quarter of a million dollars would have failed?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Super Tecmo Bug

claims.claim_text: Roof-mounted panels on a car top out around 800 watts, which yields too little daily energy to sustain continuous driving even with full sun in the Australian outback.
claims.quote_verbatim: cause it's only got 800 Watts worth of solar panels. Right. And if you just run the numbers, 800 Watts doesn't put much energy per day into your EV.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Works on my machine

claims.claim_text: When a feeder carries more distributed solar than local load can absorb, the first tool available to a utility is curtailment of that generation.
claims.quote_verbatim: So there's three answers to that question. One is the utility can curtail it.
claims.speaker: Ari Gerstman
claims.episode_title: Renewable Energy Policy with Ari Gerstman

claims.claim_text: Power from a rooftop array reaches a neighbor with only a short hop because both premises sit on the same distribution feeder; moving power between blocks instead requires routing up to the substation and back down.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's making the hop because you and your neighbor are on the same feeder.
claims.speaker: Ari Gerstman
claims.episode_title: Renewable Energy Policy with Ari Gerstman

claims.claim_text: The duck curve arises because solar supply peaks hours before demand peaks, and managing that mismatch is a principal justification for deploying storage.
claims.quote_verbatim: managing the duck curve, which is, you know, the fact that all of the solar comes on supply way earlier than when peak demand is
claims.speaker: Ari Gerstman
claims.episode_title: Renewable Energy Policy with Ari Gerstman

claims.claim_text: Getting permission to install a residential array can be easy while getting authorization to operate is the hard part, because the utility's underlying requirement is retaining the ability to shut the system off when a feeder has more supply than load.
claims.quote_verbatim: But really what their concerns are is that they're going to be able to shut the thing off.
claims.speaker: Ari Gerstman
claims.episode_title: Renewable Energy Policy with Ari Gerstman

claims.claim_text: A plausible utility arrangement pays homeowners a monthly premium plus a negotiated rate in exchange for contractual rights over their battery, such as requiring at least 50 percent state of charge at 6pm in summer and unrestricted draw from it.
claims.quote_verbatim: now your battery must be at least at 50% capacity and we're allowed to take as much of it as we want
claims.speaker: Ari Gerstman
claims.episode_title: Renewable Energy Policy with Ari Gerstman

claims.claim_text: A solar-diverting EV charger senses export with current clamps and starts charging the car once surplus exceeds a set threshold, keeping the energy on site instead of exporting it at the low feed-in rate.
claims.quote_verbatim: So as soon as it goes excess by a certain amount, it'll start charging your car if you've actually plugged it in.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Pseudo Code...Pseudo Good

claims.claim_text: For a household without panels but with solar neighbors who are out during the day, charging an EV at midday draws from the most local, lowest-impedance source rather than from distant generation.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because the power is going to come from the most local, lowest impedance source.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Good Energy Citizen

claims.claim_text: Solar thermal panels that circulate water through roof plumbing add cost and complexity and shift the failure mode from an electrical callout to a plumbing one.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then if one of your solar panels fails, you've got to call a plumber instead of a solar guy.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Turtles as a Service

claims.claim_text: A heat-pump hot water system uses so little energy, about three kilowatt-hours a day, that it is roughly a tenth of what a domestic PV array makes even on a winter day at thirty kilowatt-hours, which removes the case for solar thermal.
claims.quote_verbatim: to the tune of three kilowatt hours of energy a day just to heat my hot water. As a baseline, my solar system, even in winter the other day, made 30 kilowatt hours. So it's one tenth.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Turtles as a Service

claims.claim_text: A large array with battery storage can still leave twenty kilowatt-hours a day of unusable surplus coming out of winter, showing that storage sized for the house does not absorb all generation.
claims.quote_verbatim: I store it, and I've still got tons of excess. And we're just out of winter here. I'm still pissing away 20 kilowatts hours a day.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Watt Is The Deal

claims.claim_text: Timer-scheduled surplus loads fail on overcast days because the timer has no knowledge of actual generation, so the load ends up draining the house battery instead of consuming surplus.
claims.quote_verbatim: But in the last couple of days, including today, it's like, it's really overcast. So there's no excess solar at all. So I don't want to pull that energy from my battery.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Troubleshooting is the skill

claims.claim_text: Roof orientation determines which part of the day an array produces: a west-facing main roof yields only afternoon sun, so a smaller but due-south, tree-free garage roof can be the better mounting surface.
claims.quote_verbatim: The biggest part of the roof is pointed west. So it would only be afternoon sun for the main part. But the garage actually has a pretty decent sized roof as well. And that faces due south
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Tandy Train

claims.claim_text: Wholesale price and demand traces show sharp evening spikes around 5pm to 5:30pm as households return and switch on cooktops just as solar output collapses, which is when expensive peaking plant must be started.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're around about 5 p.m something like that 5 30 so people have come home from work they turned on everything right they turned on all their cooktops and everything
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Like a steam engine in your house

claims.claim_text: A 12.5 kilowatt-hour home battery is roughly equivalent to a single Powerwall, while a 25 kilowatt-hour bank is still small against an electric car pack of 38 to 58 kilowatt-hours.
claims.quote_verbatim: so that's equivalent to a single uh power wall for example for those that plan long at home it is oh it literally is a power yeah okay right
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: It Works With Option Number 5

claims.claim_text: For commercial spacecraft, solar is effectively the only practical power source because flying an RTG requires presidential-level authorization and the plutonium supply is constrained by nuclear arms treaties.
claims.quote_verbatim: for commercial missions, solar is kind of the only game in town. Um, so getting an RTG into orbit requires like the president to sign something.
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey
claims.episode_title: Electric Propulsion with Todd Bailey

claims.claim_text: A relatively small home battery is enough to bridge the evening dip: one system stops importing around noon and does not draw from the grid again until 8 or 9pm.
claims.quote_verbatim: I usually stop using power around noon, given where my panels are. And I don't start using power again from the grid till, like, 8 or 9 p.m.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Test Point Accupuncture

claims.claim_text: Australia's surplus midday solar prompted a two billion dollar national subsidy scheme to put a battery in every home, because the grid has nowhere else to absorb the excess.
claims.quote_verbatim: the new government, just announced the $2 billion battery scheme where everyone gets a battery
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Test Point Accupuncture

claims.claim_text: Solar oversupply is really a storage shortage: with enough grid storage, such as pumped hydro using hills and water, the same generation would not be a problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think there's too much solar, but there's too much solar if there's not enough grid storage. Right? If there was like, if you guys had like a lot of hills and like water that you could pump up and down it, then it would be fine.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Test Point Accupuncture

attribution_notes: ep=52: header lists speaker=Dave Jones for a passage that contains both the rooftop-vs-utility-scale cost argument and a detailed crystalline-silicon process walkthrough. The chemistry walkthrough (sand + coal, silane, deposition rods, boule, zone refining) is guest Jeri Ellsworth describing semiconductor chemical processing, which is the episode's subject; attributed to Ellsworth. The cost-benefit framing is attributed to Dave Jones.

ep=127/150/249/524/580/606/610/612/674/677/683: Australian rooftop-solar, feed-in-tariff and home-system details are attributed to Dave Jones by content (he is the Sydney-based host with the installed system), regardless of the header label on any given passage.

ep=127 passage [6] is labelled speaker=Chris Gammell but contains Dave Jones describing Sydney weather and the $4k 1.5 kW system; the AC-peak/solar-coincidence observation is Chris Gammell. Split by content.

ep=206 is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE throughout. Passages [18]-[22] mix Martin Lorton (South African solar experiments, Cleveland install, no grid feed-in from his utility) with Dave Jones (8 cent Australian feed-in, changed daytime habits). Attributed by content, not by header, including passage [22] whose header says Dave Jones but whose first half is Martin.
ep=518 passage [44] header says Chris Gammell, but the power-budget and duty-cycle statements are guest Joris Aerts describing his own satellite design. Attributed to Joris Aerts.
ep=540 passage [46] header says Fran Blanche, but the payback-period explanation is clearly Dave Jones answering Fran's remark about his videos. Attributed to Dave Jones.

ep=555, 561, 565, 666, 688, 702: several passages carry a Dave Jones header while the speaker is plainly Chris Gammell (US roof, US solar salesperson friend, cold-weather gel-cell build, US battery/grid-mix figures). Attributed by content; where the exchange is genuinely two-way inside one quote, speaker is set to the person whose words the quote reproduces.
ep=630 is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE across all passages; the policy/grid explanations are guest Ari Gerstman and the questions are Chris Gammell. Attributed by content.

ep=702 passage [99] header says Dave Jones; the 'too much solar if there's not enough grid storage' / pumped-hydro remark is Chris Gammell responding to Dave's uptake comment. Attributed to Chris Gammell.
ep=232 passages are headed Bob Davidson and the energy-harvesting content matches his own sensor work; kept as Bob Davidson.
ep=329: passage [30] is headed Chris Gammell and passage [31] Chris White, but the cost-per-watt/market-inevitability line is Dave Jones responding; attributed to Dave Jones by content.
